title: Are good samaritan laws effective?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine Good Samaritan laws: their origin in the Gospel of Luke parable, the patchwork of state laws in the US, common elements (no compensation, no recklessness, often limited to untrained helpers doing CPR or bleeding control), duty-to-act laws (Vermont, California, Michigan, Argentina), the California Lisa Torti and Alexandra van Horn car-rescue lawsuit, China's Peng Yu bus case and the resulting bystander chilling effect, the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act, college medical amnesty (Lifeline/911) laws, and naloxone (Narcan) good Samaritan protections. Also discusses the Seinfeld finale and the Kitty Genovese bystander effect as context. Ends with listener mail from Jane in Seattle.

segments.title: Opening banter and Kitty Genovese setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of Good Samaritan laws, referencing the Kitty Genovese case and the bystander effect, and noting that Good Samaritan laws are not actually a result of that case.

segments.title: Origins of the name: the Good Samaritan parable
segments.summary: The hosts recount the Gospel of Luke parable in which a Samaritan helps a robbed and injured Jewish man, explaining the origin of the name. They describe the state-by-state patchwork of laws covering all fifty states and D.C.

segments.title: Common elements and variations by state
segments.summary: Core features shared across laws: no compensation for aid and no reckless or negligent conduct. Examples include Oklahoma's limits to untrained helpers doing CPR or stopping bleeding, defibrillator coverage, Vermont's fine for bystanders who do nothing, and Michigan's protections for block parents and ski patrol.

segments.title: Duty to act laws in Argentina
segments.summary: Argentina may impose jail time for endangering or abandoning a person in need, and the hosts discuss the fine line involved.

segments.title: Lisa Torti and Alexandra van Horn California case
segments.summary: Coworkers Lisa Torti and Alexandra van Horn went out for drinks; after van Horn crashed, Torti pulled her from the car believing it might explode, leaving her paralyzed. The California Supreme Court ruled Torti could be sued because the protection covered only medical care; the legislature then amended the law to include non-medical emergency care. The case involved car insurance disputes and reportedly settled for four million dollars.
topics: Lisa Torti Alexandra van Horn case

segments.title: China's Peng Yu case and chilling effect on helping
segments.summary: In 2006 Peng Yu was sued by an elderly woman he had helped after she fell getting off a bus; the court found him responsible. The case fueled a Chinese culture of reluctance to help, with people leaving injured people in the street. China passed a national Good Samaritan law in 2017, which the hosts say may go too far in some cases.

segments.title: Food donation and college medical amnesty laws
segments.summary: The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act protects food donors from liability after the mid-1990s food waste concern. Lifeline and 911 medical amnesty laws at about thirty universities protect underage drinkers who call for help, and similar protections cover overdose calls involving opioids, with naloxone (Narcan) kits used by civilians.

segments.title: Duty to act vs Seinfeld finale
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish duty to act from Good Samaritan laws, noting the Seinfeld finale gang would likely not have been jailed under most duty-to-act laws, and discuss the difficulty of ending Seinfeld.

segments.title: Listener mail from Jane in Seattle
segments.summary: Jane describes listening to the show during a night watch on a sailing trip from Seattle to San Diego, and thanks the hosts for comfort after her brother's death.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to ways to get in touch.
